items.title: Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee Type I knees are not a homogeneous phenotype : differences in coronal alignment sensitivity following total knee arthroplasty.
items.summary: Aims The Coronal Plane Alignment of the Knee (CPAK) classification categorizes knees into nine phenotypes based on the arithmetic hip-knee-ankle angle (aHKA) and joint line obliquity (JLO). CPAK Type I is highly prevalent in East Asian populations, but encompasses a broad spectrum of varus deformity. We hypothesized that CPAK Type I knees are not a homogeneous phenotype, and that the severity of constitutional varus may modify the relationship between coronal alignment changes and clinical outcomes after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Methods This retrospective study included 258 knees undergoing primary TKA using navigation with a mechanical alignment strategy. CPAK Type I knees were sub-classified into Type 0 (aHKA Results Across all knees, ΔJLO and ΔaHKA were not associated with KOOS outcomes.
items.author: Kawaguchi K, Yamagami R, Kono K, Young SW, Tay ML, Taketomi S, Inui H, Tanaka S.

items.title: Distinct input-output relationships between basal forebrain subnuclei underlie heterogeneous cholinergic modulation of the mouse cortex
items.summary: The basal forebrain (BF) supports many behavioral functions via its brain-wide projections, which can be recruited independently and task specifically. However, the anatomical underpinnings for this functional heterogeneity are poorly understood. Here, we compared two mouse BF subnuclei, the horizontal diagonal band (HDB) and the substantial innominata (SI), in terms of their anatomical connectivity and functional recruitment. Using anterograde and retrograde tracing, we show that they target largely segregated forebrain regions, but their input comes from a partially overlapping subset of regions. However, many neurons within each region project to just one of the subnuclei, suggesting they can be recruited independently.
items.author: Tan, J., Harter, A. M., Kolb, M. et al.

items.title: Visual object recognition in the fly: the internal representation of a predator drives defensive behaviour
items.summary: Animals recognize visual objects and respond to them appropriately to survive. This process is thought to unfold in stages: the visual scene is first deconstructed into constituent features, which are then reconstructed into representations of object identity and relayed to motor circuits. Here we define a neural circuit in Drosophila that underlies the visual recognition of a natural predator, the parasitoid wasp, and orchestrates defence. We found that flies exhibit a repertoire of directed defensive actions structured by the wasp's position within the fly's field of view. Expression of these behaviours is driven by visual detection of a conspicuous morphological cue -- the wasp's elongated antennae.
items.author: Denagamage, S., Foltz, M., Dalstein, V. M. et al.

items.title: Clofarabine enforces dual host-pathogen translational arrest and disarms enteric bacterial virulence
items.summary: Enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC/EHEC) cause severe global diarrhoeal disease, exacerbated by rising antimicrobial resistance. Pathogenesis relies on attaching and effacing lesions, where bacteria generate actin pedestals to adhere, replicate, and destroy intestinal microvilli. To identify novel anti-virulence candidates targeting this process, we conducted a high-throughput phenotypic screen quantifying pedestal formation via high-content fluorescence microscopy. We identified the anticancer nucleotide analogue clofarabine as a potent inhibitor of EPEC growth and pathogenesis. Distinct from its oncology mechanism - inducing DNA chain termination and apoptosis - clofarabine competes with bacterial ATP-dependent processes to impede gene transcription, protein synthesis, and Type III Secretion System (T3SS) function.
items.author: Deans, N. D., Naylor, K. L., Srour, S. et al.

items.title: Reliable prediction of short linear motifs in the human proteome
items.summary: Short linear motifs (SLiMs) are small interaction modules within intrinsically disordered regions of proteins that interact with specific domains, and thereby regulate diverse biological processes. The limited information in SLiM definitions leads to frequent false positive hits in computational and experimental SLiM identification methods. Here, we refined the annotations of known motif classes to create a high-quality training dataset, and developed SLiMMine, a deep learning-based method to identify SLiMs in the human proteome. Relying on protein embeddings, SLiMMine outperforms similar approaches in identifying functional SLiMs, while eliminating ~80% of the pattern matching-based hits as false-positives. Furthermore, it can uncover novel SLiMs that do not fit known motif classes purely based on sequence features.
items.author: Pancsa, R., Ficho, E., Kalman, Z. E. et al.

items.title: Coupling Complementary Pathways in a Bacterial Co-culture Enables 4-Aminophenol Removal during Paracetamol Degradation
items.summary: Pharmaceutical biodegradation can generate potentially toxic metabolites that persist after the parent compound has been removed, posing additional risks to aquatic environments. Microbial co-cultures offer a promising strategy to address this challenge by combining complementary metabolic capabilities to remove both pharmaceuticals and their harmful transformation products by coupling complementary degradation pathways. Here, we investigated a two-species co-culture combining the paracetamol-degrading bacterium Delftia P1 with Microbacterium lacus to enable subsequent 4-AP removal. While Delftia P1 efficiently degraded paracetamol, it accumulated 4-AP as a dead-end metabolite. M. lacus was selected to complement this metabolic limitation because its genome contains a homolog of sadB, a monooxygenase gene involved in 4-AP transformation.
items.author: Demaria, F., Schaffter, M., Zimmardi, C. et al.

items.title: Infection-dependent antibiotic response phenotypes emerge during chronic airway adaptation of Pseudomonas aeruginosa
items.summary: Objectives Chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway infections can persist for years despite intensive antibiotic therapy guided by standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing. While this technique captures the emergence of resistance, it does not reproduce many features of the infection environment, where adaptation acquired during chronic infection may alter bacterial responses to antibiotics in ways that are not fully reflected by conventional susceptibility testing. Here we investigated antibiotic responses of longitudinal clinical isolates under standard laboratory conditions and in an airway epithelial infection model. Methods Six longitudinal pairs of P. aeruginosa isolates from people with cystic fibrosis were analysed. Changes in bacterial growth following exposure to tobramycin, ceftazidime and ciprofloxacin were quantified under standard laboratory conditions and compared with changes in bacterial burden after treatment measured in differentiated airway epithelial cultures maintained under air-liquid interface (ALI) conditions that reproduce key features of the airway infection environment.
items.author: Laborda, P., Cebrian-Sastre, E., La Rosa, R. et al.

items.title: Flexible phosphorus allocation to the phosphoproteome underpins diatom regulatory adaptations to fluctuating phosphate supply
items.summary: Diatoms are major drivers of marine phosphorus (P) cycling and are highly adapted to cope with variable P supply. P-starved diatoms can sense increases in P availability within seconds, accumulating this limiting resource through luxury polyphosphate (polyP) storage. Yet, how diatoms coordinate such responses is unknown. Protein phosphorylation is a core mechanism for environmental signal transduction in eukaryotes, but how cells balance investment in protein phosphorylation against competing physiological demands during P limitation is poorly understood. Here, we characterise system-wide remodelling of the Phaeodactylum tricornutum phosphoproteome in response to P deficiency and subsequent resupply. We identify widespread proteome dephosphorylation across 44% of phosphosites, revealing a previously unrecognised P-sparing strategy in marine phytoplankton.
items.author: Meeda, Y., Touhami, Y., Wharam, S. et al.

items.title: Engineered Miniature ParTasR Enables Efficient PAMless Genome Editing
items.summary: TIGR-Tas system holds great promise for genome-engineering applications owing to its compact size and PAMless targeting capability. However, its low editing efficiency in mammalian cells severely limits its broader utility. Here, we engineered a highly active variant of ParTasR, termed eTasR, through structure-guided rational design of ParTasR combined with co-expression of the 3'[->]5' exonuclease TREX2. eTasR increased editing efficiency in mammalian cells from the original average 4.29% to 48.94% with an average 26.52-fold improvement, substantially outperforming the popular PAM-free version of nuclease-SpRY. Moreover, a single AAV delivery of eTasR in vivo effectively alleviates the disease phenotype of hereditary tyrosinemia type I (HT1) mouse model through targeted Hpd editing.
items.author: Zhang, X., Zhu, Q., Zhang, Z. et al.

items.title: Positive selection tends to act on exposed extracellular regions and delineate interaction modules targeted by pathogens
items.summary: Background: Positive selection shapes protein function by favoring amino acid substitutions that increase fitness. Although numerous studies have identified positively selected genes (PSGs), the structural principles underlying residue-level positive selection remain incompletely understood and previous studies have produced conflicting conclusions, particularly regarding the preferential location of positively selected residues (PSRs) within intrinsically disordered regions. In order to resolve these issues and to better understand the driving forces underlying positive selection in human proteins, we performed a comprehensive analysis on a manually curated, high quality collection of PSGs and PSRs as well as on a large-scale PSR dataset restricted to proteins with experimental structures.
items.author: Dobson, L., Schad, E., Ficho, E. et al.

items.title: Parallel enterocyte caspase and cytokine responses couple hypoxia to reoxygenation-dependent intestinal regeneration in Drosophila
items.summary: Intestinal oxygen availability fluctuates during both normal physiology and disease, yet how the intestinal epithelium adapts to these changing environments remains poorly understood. Using the adult Drosophila intestine, we show that hypoxia and reoxygenation drive distinct phases of an epithelial damage and repair response. Hypoxia induces two parallel responses in largely separate enterocyte populations: an AMPK-p53-dependent response that primes enterocytes for apoptosis, and an independent Upd cytokine response that activates JAK-STAT signaling in intestinal stem cells (ISCs). Despite activation of both pathways during hypoxia, neither apoptosis nor ISC proliferation occurs until oxygen is restored. Upon reoxygenation, enterocyte loss and ISC proliferation proceed together and both are required for recovery of intestinal length.
items.author: Bodkhe, P., Ding, K., Grewal, S. S.

items.title: Age-dependent mechanical stress underlies unexpected vestibular differentiation and regeneration patterns
items.summary: Loss of inner-ear sensory hair cells (HCs) is a major cause of hearing and balance disorders. Promoting HC regeneration offers a potential therapeutic strategy, but regenerative capacity is limited in adult mammals and declines rapidly during early postnatal development in mice. HCs can regenerate through trans-differentiation of neighboring supporting cells in a process controlled by Notch mediated lateral inhibition. However, the factors underlying the decrease in regeneration capacity are poorly understood. Here, we combine live imaging with single-HC ablation in mouse vestibular explants to track the dynamics of HC development and regeneration. We reveal unexpected age-dependent deviations from the classical lateral inhibition model, in which new HCs differentiate adjacent to existing HCs.
items.author: Inbar Kasirer, S., Shraga, M., Dullweber, T. et al.

items.title: Beaver Impacts Tool: A Graphical User Interface for Analyzing Ecosystem Impacts of Beaver Dams Using Remote Sensing Data
items.summary: Beavers are being increasingly recognized as driving factors in diverse and resilient riparian ecosystems. Many of their impacts, including changes to water levels and vegetation, can be studied through remote sensing. However, ecologists and conservationists may lack the tools to easily analyze remote sensing data for these purposes. We offer here a Google Earth Engine-backed Streamlit app that allows users to easily upload locations of observed dams or installed beaver dam analogs for analysis. Via a graphical user interface, users then generate a set of dam-absent locations for comparison and receive plots and numerical data indicating how indices associated with vegetation, water, temperature, and evapotranspiration change over time for dam-present and dam-absent locations.
items.author: Tyree, Q., Etheredge, J., Kong, Z. et al.

items.title: Characterizing the Prey Landscape of Endangered Cook Inlet Beluga Whales Using an eDNA Time Series
items.summary: Our ability to understand habitat utilization in the context of foraging, prey dynamics, and anthropogenic disturbance is critical for the effective management of protected species globally. Here we examine the occurrence of the endangered Cook Inlet beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas) in the context of seasonally changing prey fields by leveraging quantitative eDNA metabarcoding approaches. Specifically, eDNA approaches were used to generate estimates of fish abundances using a joint modeling framework that derives total DNA concentration from a coho (Oncorhynchus kisutch) qPCR assay and bias-corrected proportional abundance of multiple salmonid species using MiFish 12S metabarcoding of environmental and mock community samples.
items.author: Gold, Z., Shelton, A., Tobin, D. D. B. et al.

items.title: Manuscript, raw data, and R code: Ziziphus spina-christi as a Refuge and Resource for Parasitoids in Arid Ecosystems
items.summary: 1. Climate change is increasing aridity in dryland ecosystems, potentially threatening parasitoid wasps through reduced resource availability and environmental stress. Native drought-adapted plants may help sustain parasitoid communities by providing floral resources and refuge habitats. The tree Ziziphus spina-christi (L.) tolerates drought and heat stress, making it a promising candidate species for desert afforestation and dryland restoration. Its abundant flowering attracts a wide range of insects, supports honey production, and provides valuable forage resources for pollinators. 2. In this two-year study, we investigated the role of Ziziphus spina-christi in supporting parasitoid wasps across four sites that span a 200-600 mm annual rainfall gradient.
items.author: Saabna, N., Keasar, T.

items.title: Rapid estimation of insect biodiversity using AI assisted image analysis:a cost-effective tool for monitoring and ecological assessmen
items.summary: Protection of natural areas and environmentally friendly management of anthropogenic landscapes require reliable tools for monitoring and comparing biodiversity. Bioindicator-based approaches can support large-scale ecological assessment, but insect monitoring remains constrained by the taxonomic expertise required for species identification. Here, we propose an AI-supported index for estimating the biodiversity of flying insects, based on the diversity of visual features of insect bodies. Flying insects were captured using yellow sticky traps across agricultural and natural habitats, seasons, crops, and sites in Israel's Mediterranean region. Traps were scanned at high resolution and uploaded to a dedicated image database. A machine learning model was used to detect and delineate insects, after which engineered visual features representing body size, color, and shape were extracted.
items.author: Cabra-Leykin, L., Keasar, T., Keasar, C.

items.title: Disturbance increases diversity by weakening competition rather than reducing intrinsic population growth
items.summary: Physical disturbance is pervasive across ecosystems. However, why it can increase diversity remains unresolved. For over five decades, two hypotheses have highlighted contrasting mechanisms: weakened heterospecific competition, or reduced intrinsic demographic rates that slow competitive exclusion. Here, we formalize these largely verbal hypotheses using standard models of multispecies community dynamics and test the resulting quantitative predictions in an experimental mesocosm system. We established 210 annual plant communities that were subject to disturbances, fit a process-based model to their dynamics, and used counterfactual simulations to disentangle mechanisms under early-season clipping during vegetative growth and late-season clipping during reproduction. Early clipping increased diversity persistently, whereas late clipping caused a transient decline.
items.author: Neumann, Y., Gross, O., Schabes, T. et al.

items.title: Genetic ancestry influences the relative expression of ancestral haplotypes within admixed individuals
items.summary: Allele-specific expression (ASE) reflects differences between the two haplotypes a person carries, but most ASE studies have been done in European-descent samples. Admixed individuals carry haplotypes from different ancestral backgrounds within the same cell, which allows ancestry effects on regulation to be measured directly. We integrated phased whole-blood RNA-seq with local ancestry inference in 779 participants from the MAGENTA cohort, including non-Hispanic White, African American, Caribbean Hispanic, and Peruvian individuals. Higher West African (YRI) ancestry proportion was associated with more ASE-positive genes per person, and the association remained after adjusting for age, sex, Alzheimer's disease status, APOE genotype, and the number of heterozygous genes.
items.author: vazquez-hidalgo, e., Mews, M. A., Gomez, L. et al.

items.title: MicroDUET: a dual-headed genomic foundation model for pathogen surveillance
items.summary: Pathogen genomic surveillance works from raw reads, assembled genomes and alignments, representations that are slow and costly to compare at scale. Compact embeddings from genomic language models offer an alternative, but surveillance requires resolving both evolutionary ancestry (phylogeny) and phenotypic capability (function) - which need not co-vary. Here we present MicroDUET, which adapts a 26.6-million-parameter ProkBERT backbone with two 3.5-million-parameter adapter heads: a phylogeny head trained contrastively on genome windows from the same microbes, and a function head trained to identify genes across taxa. On held-out retrieval benchmarks, the phylogeny head returned the correct species for 80.3% and 66.6% of cellular and viral queries, and the function head the correct gene family for 97.3% and 97.2%, reaching 74.4% accuracy on an independent antimicrobial resistance-class benchmark.
items.author: Barber, M., Suster, C. J. E., Lei, J. et al.

items.title: Social hierarchy assays measure independent features of competitive ability
items.summary: In social species, hierarchies emerge across diverse behavioral contexts, including dyadic contests, resource competition, and territorial marking. Whether competitive success generalizes across these contexts remains unclear, in part because individual performance and hierarchy structure are difficult to compare directly across assays. Here, we establish a framework for such comparisons using three behavioral paradigms (the tube test, the warm spot assay, and the void spot assay) in same-sex triads of BALB/c and C57BL/6 mice, as well as Shank3B knockouts, which exhibit impaired social recognition. Hierarchies emerged in all three assays, but their structure and behavioral determinants differed by strain and sex.
items.author: Pitesky, R., Wade, M., Fanelli, R. E. et al.

items.title: Proteomic Evaluation of the Progression from Acute Kidney Injury to Chronic Kidney Disease
items.summary: Acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are interconnected syndromes with substantial global burden, yet the molecular mechanisms driving the transition from acute injury to chronic fibrosis remain incompletely understood. We performed quantitative data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS) proteomics on mouse models of AKI (ischemia-reperfusion injury) and CKD (unilateral ureteral obstruction), quantifying 5,985 protein groups. A conserved core injury response of 1,475 shared proteins (46%) was dominated by mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of solute transporters, and immune and extracellular matrix remodeling. AKI was marked by chromatin reorganization, DNA damage response, and acute inflammation, whereas CKD showed sustained fibrosis, complement activation, and coagulation.
items.author: Sims-Lucas, S., Bons, J., Pfister, K. E. et al.

items.title: Spatiotemporal multiplexing on subretinal prosthesis increases selectivity of the network-mediated stimulation
items.summary: Subretinal photovoltaic implants (PRIMA) provide form vision in patients blinded by age-related macular degeneration. The success of this approach is attributed in part to the network-mediated stimulation, which preserves many features of the natural retinal signal encoding. For efficient stimulation of bipolar cells (BC) with smaller pixels, electric field confinement should be relaxed, yet direct activation of the retinal ganglion cells (RGC) should be avoided. Here we present a new method for selective stimulation of bipolar cells using image multiplexing - sequential presentation of the image's components in several subframes. With sizes of the subframe islands optimized by computational modelling, the selectivity of network (BC) mediated retinal stimulation increased over 5 times in rats.
items.author: Jensen, N., Ly, K., Pham-Howard, D. et al.

items.title: Machine learning assisted multi-level differentiation of blood cells using multi-frequency electro-mechanical impedance cytometry
items.summary: We report a multi-frequency microfluidic impedance cytometer with multimodal measurement of electrical and mechanical cell properties. Using the large feature set from the multimodality, we implemented machine learning assisted differentiation of cells. We have demonstrated a constriction-equipped channel to study the mechanical cell properties, and integrated multiple microelectrodes that capture electric field information pertaining to various stages of cell transit. Our system works over a wide frequency range from 800 kHz to 8 MHz. We developed a machine learning workflow to classify cells using our multi-modal data. Using this platform to show blood cell differentiation, our system shows minimum F1 score to be 0.92, minimizing both false negatives and false positives, which is important for medical diagnosis.
items.author: Bansal, I., Suresh, S. K., Sagar, N. et al.

items.title: Affinity-guided design of PDZ-binding peptides in a shared latent space
items.summary: PDZ-binding motifs (PBMs) are short C-terminal sequences that bind PDZ domains and contribute to protein localization and complex assembly. Designing PBMs could modulate these interactions while leaving most of the original protein sequence unchanged. Because PDZ recognition preferences overlap, modulating intended interactions requires considering off-target binding alongside target affinity. Computational PBM design methods generally use sequence-based affinity prediction and structure-based evaluation, but it remains challenging to guide sequence searches toward different binding objectives with a single trained model. Here, we propose a deep learning-based method to design PBMs by analytically formulating single-target, off-target-aware, and dual-target design objectives as directions in a PDZ-PBM shared latent space learned through quantitative PDZ-PBM affinity prediction.
items.author: Yamahata, I., Shimamura, T., Hayashi, S.

items.title: Evaluating speech-like distortion product otoacoustic emissions: a comparison of time- and frequency-domain metrics across three datasets
items.summary: Speech-like distortion-product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs) allow cochlear activity to be measured during the perception of natural, continuous speech and have been used to study attentional effects in the cochlea. The technique is still young, however, and existing studies differ in stimulus design and in the metric used to quantify the emissions, which makes their results difficult to compare. Here, we reanalysed three existing datasets (106 participants, 14 stimulus types) with a common pipeline. We compared six metrics: the band power of the recording, the magnitude-squared coherence (MSC) between the recording and a DPOAE template, and four metrics derived from their complex cross-correlation, namely peak magnitude, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), peak area and peak width.
items.author: Steinebach, J., Reichenbach, T.

items.title: DNA Sequence Differentially Modulates Histone Core and Tail Interactions in Canonical and Centromeric Nucleosomes
items.summary: Human centromeric chromatin is a specialized chromatin domain characterized by CENP-A-containing nucleosomes interspersed with canonical histone H3 nucleosomes. It is assembled on tandem repeats of -satellite DNA and defines centromere identity. How histone variant identity and DNA sequence jointly shape nucleosome structure and histone-DNA interactions that underpin centromeric chromatin formation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the structural plasticity of the histone core and nucleosomal DNA, histone tail dynamics and DNA-sequence dependent changes for canonical (H3) and centromeric (CENP-A) nucleosomes using the SIRAH coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CG-MD) simulations. Nucleosomes containing -satellite positioning sequence (ASP) and Widom 601 DNA sequence are systematically analyzed and compared.
items.author: Ghosh Moulick, A., Erhardt, S., Kozlowska, M.

items.title: Epigenomic circuits shaping cellular heterogeneity in pleural mesothelioma
items.summary: Pleural mesothelioma (PM) is an aggressive and lethal malignancy with current treatments offering limited clinical benefit. In this study, we utilized single-cell chromatin accessibility and transcriptomic profiling of patient-matched samples to infer the epigenomic regulation underlying cellular heterogeneity in PM. High-resolution epigenomic profiling suggested transcriptional regulators with putative pro-tumoral roles in mesothelioma, whose function was experimentally tested using genetic perturbations across four PM cell lines. Furthermore, we observed several putative associations between epigenomic circuits and macrophage ontogeny, a sarcomatoid-like neoplastic state, and a fetal-like endothelial cell state. Our analysis also showed similarities between the chromatin accessibility landscapes of exhausted CD8 T and KLRC1 natural killer cells and identified NR4A2 as a potential shared regulator of dysfunction in both lymphocyte subsets.
items.author: Tsankov, A., Giotti, B., Chang, L. et al.

items.title: Galectin-1 identifies a unique subpopulation of highly invasive glioblastoma cells and enables their migration.
items.summary: Glioblastoma (GBM), the most common primary brain tumor, is characterized by extensive infiltration into surrounding brain tissue. GBM tumors exhibit substantial intratumoral heterogeneity making it difficult to identify and target invasive cell subpopulations. Here, we use an in vitro model of the mechanical transitions at the tumor-brain interface to isolate highly invasive GBM cells from populations derived from unique patient tumors. Using single-cell RNA sequencing combined with cell barcodes we were able to trace distinct cell lineages during migration and identify an invasive subpopulation which preferentially migrates across stiffness interfaces. This mechanically sensitive invasive subpopulation exhibits a transcriptomic profile characterized by overexpression of galectin-1, a {beta}-galactoside binding protein.
items.author: Sanazzaro, T., Cotner, M., Arvinth, N. et al.

items.title: Advancing AOPs for genotoxicity through quantifying KERs linking DNA alkylation to increase in mutations and chromosome aberrations
items.summary: Quantitative Adverse Outcome Pathways (qAOPs) help translate mechanistic knowledge into quantitative toxicity predictions; however, their development is constrained by the limited availability and heterogeneity of quantitative data. Here, we investigated the feasibility of developing a qAOP for genotoxicity by modeling quantitative relationships linking DNA alkylation to increased mutations and structural chromosome aberrations through intermediate biological key events (KEs). We compiled and harmonized published concentration-response data from human lymphoblastoid TK6 cells exposed to ethyl methanesulfonate, methyl methanesulfonate, or N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea, covering eight genotoxicity assays representing five KEs with well-established dependencies. We evaluated sources of variability, compared points of departure (PoDs), and quantified relationships between successive events using response-response modeling.
items.author: Winkelman, L. M. T., Demuynck, E., Bryce, S. M. et al.

items.title: The canine hair metabolome encodes age and coat exposure in over 700 dogs
items.summary: Hair can be collected noninvasively and stored for years, making it a practical sample for studying physiology and environmental exposure. Yet the chemical information it carries in dogs remains largely unexplored. We profiled 782 banked hair samples from 700 Golden Retrievers by untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, detecting 4,533 compound groups and revealing an unexpectedly rich chemical profile. Prominent signals reflected skin-surface and hair chemistry, including amino acids, peptides and urocanic acid, alongside surfactants, plasticizers and pesticides detectable despite washing. A signal annotated as imidacloprid distinguished dogs receiving topical products containing this insecticide from dogs receiving no flea or tick preventive (AUC 0.865).
items.author: Chaudhry, F., Ficaro, L., Rodrick, T. et al.

items.title: Dietary Human HSP90 Promotes Longevity and Healthspan in Caenorhabditis elegans via a Multi-Branched Stress Signaling Pathway
items.summary: The loss of proteostasis is one of the primary drivers of aging. Despite the important role of the molecular chaperone HSP90 in maintaining proteostasis, its systemic role in aging appears contradictory because its inhibitors can effectively extend lifespan across diverse species. This study showed that dietary HSP90 supplementation via Escherichia coli significantly extended lifespan and healthspan of Caenorhabditis elegans without fertility trade-offs. Exogenous HSP90 likely acts as an extracellular signaling ligand that engages downstream kinase networks to drive the activation of three major longevity-associated transcription factors: DAF-16, SKN-1, and HSF-1. In addition, we demonstrated the additive effect of combining dietary HSP90 supplementation with the senolytic HSP90 inhibitor tanespimycin, indicating that extracellular proteostatic signaling and the intracellular inhibition of HSP90 can work together to enhance longevity.

items.title: Contrastive local learning in large nonlinear analog circuits
items.summary: Machine learning in physical hardware promises to reduce training cost by colocating computation, memory and adaptation within device physics. Contrastive local learning networks (CLLNs) offer a compelling route: an electrical circuit relaxes to equilibrium in free and weakly clamped states, and each adaptive element updates from local voltage contrasts rather than backpropagated error signals. Yet whether nonlinear transistor implementations can scale beyond proof-of-concept circuits, and what design principles control that scaling, have remained unknown. Here we show that nonlinear analog circuits trained by contrastive local rules can learn larger machine-learning tasks and remain robust under hardware nonidealities. Using device-level circuit simulations, we systematically explore initialization, operating regime, loss-dependent clamping and training parameters, and scale CLLNs beyond ten thousand adaptive edges.
